flawed_step: To prove uniqueness, you would need distinct arc capacities to force distinct cut capacities. That step fails. Two different vertex sets S can have exactly the same set of crossing arcs, which happens when a vertex has no arcs. The definitions explicitly allow isolated vertices. Even without them, sums of different sets of arcs can be equal.
counterexample: Vertices: V = {s, t, a, b}. There is one arc, s->t, with capacity 1. The capacities are pairwise distinct because there is only one arc. The graph has no loops, and a and b are isolated, which the definitions permit. The maximum flow is 1, which is positive. The s-t cuts are S = {s}, {s,a}, {s,b} and {s,a,b}. In every case, the only arc going from S to V\S is s->t, so every cut has capacity 1. All four cuts are therefore minimum cuts, so the minimum cut is not unique.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Distinct arc capacities do not make the minimum cut unique, because different vertex sets can be crossed by exactly the same arcs. In the 4-vertex example, s->t has capacity 1 and a, b are isolated. The max flow is 1, and there are four minimum cuts, each of capacity 1.
